topic.title: The ticket is for the outing, not the film
topic.claim: We don't buy a Rs 2,600 recliner seat to watch a film, we buy it to be seen having the best seat, and the review comes after.
topic.behaviour: Premium IMAX recliner seats sold out in the festive rush while the same film's reviews were split on X. People book the visible upgrade before they know if the film is good.
topic.mechanism: Cinemas and booking apps price the seat, not the story. A bad film still sells the photo, the outing and the 'we went' bragging rights, so the price has no reason to wait for the verdict.
topic.group: Urban working Indians 24 to 32 who book weekend and festival outings
topic.moment: You open the booking app on a holiday, see the cheap seats gone, and tap the Rs 1,600 one anyway.

turn.believed: A higher ticket price means you expect a better film.
turn.actually: The higher price buys a better seat and a better story to tell. The film is almost beside the point.

topic.feeling: slightly foolish and also not sorry
topic.villain: a dynamic pricing model that charges for the seat when demand is highest, which is before any review exists
topic.because: Cinema chains earn most when everyone books in the first festive days. Seat tiers turn the same three hours into a status ladder you can climb with money.

proof.fact: On BookMyShow listings checked on 6 November, the top price for Ramayana was Rs 2,600 for IMAX 3D recliners at PVR Palladium Mall, Ahmedabad, while regular 2D shows started around Rs 500.

topic.payoff: Test yourself: would you still pay the recliner price if you couldn't post a single photo of it?
topic.send_to: The friend who always books the premium seat and then says the film was 'okay'.
real_details: Most premium categories sold out in the festive rush
Viewers on X were divided on release day, with some calling it 'average' and one suggesting waiting for OTT
topic.news_peg: Ramayana released on 5 November 2026 with recliner tickets listed at Rs 2,600 on 6 November and split first-day reviews
topic.why_now: The film is still in theatres and the booking-first, verdict-later pattern is playing out in real time.

score.why: Paying for the best seat is paying for the story you tell afterwards. It fits the page's belief that Indians pay for what others can see, and ends on a photo test.
